title: Why add an option few people buy?
principle: A clearly worse third option makes the one beside it sell.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a magazine called The Economist. Its website once had three yearly plans. Web only: $59. Print only: $125. Print and web together: $125. Look again. Print only cost the same as print and web.

screens.prompt: Dan Ariely, a scientist, showed these three plans to 100 students. How many picked print only?
screens.why: Nobody chose print only. Why would they? For the same $125, they could get print and web. But that plan nobody chose had a purpose. Let me show you.

screens.title: What happened next
screens.text: 84 of the 100 students chose print and web for $125. Then Ariely removed print only and asked a new group of students. Now only 32 of 100 chose print and web. The other 68 chose the cheaper $59 web plan.

screens.title: The decoy effect
screens.text: This is called the decoy effect. A decoy is a choice that is clearly worse than the one next to it. Few people buy it. But it makes the better choice look like a good deal, so more people pick it. Shops often use this on you.

screens.prompt: Popcorn costs ₹180 for small, ₹290 for medium, and ₹320 for large. Large has twice as much as medium. Which is the decoy?
screens.why: Yes. Medium costs only ₹30 less than large. So large looks like a good deal, and more people pick it. That's how a decoy works on you.

wrong.a: Small is the cheap choice, like the $59 web plan. Look at medium: ₹290, only ₹30 less than large. It makes large look like a good deal.
wrong.c: Large is the one the cinema wants you to buy. The decoy is medium: ₹290 for less popcorn, only ₹30 less than large.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: The Economist sells around the world, but your home bakery can use the same idea fairly. It's February. Families want more than a cake for birthday parties. Your cake is ₹850. You plan a party pack with 12 cupcakes, a name topper and delivery.

screens.prompt: Here are your three party plans. Which one is the decoy?
screens.why: Right. For only ₹50 more, the full pack adds a topper and delivery. Cake and cupcakes makes the full pack look like a good deal, just as print only helped sell print and web.

wrong.a: That's the plan you want families to pick. The decoy is cake and cupcakes at ₹1,400: only ₹50 less, but without a topper or delivery.
wrong.b: Cake only is the cheap choice, like the $59 web plan. The decoy is cake and cupcakes at ₹1,400: only ₹50 less than the full pack.

screens.title: Where it goes wrong
screens.text: This can fail in two ways. A decoy nobody would want looks like a trick, so buyers stop trusting you. Too many choices can also stop people from buying. In a famous jam test, many more shoppers bought from a table with 6 jams than one with 24.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six menu ideas. For each one, tell me: does it help buyers choose, or does it trick or confuse them?

items.text: Fresh cake and cupcakes at ₹1,400, a plan you're happy to sell
A ₹4,999 "royal" cake you would refuse to bake
Ten party plans, each a little different
Three plans, with the best value marked clearly
A "Value" plan with a smaller cake, but you don't tell buyers
Saying plainly what each plan includes

screens.why: A fair decoy is a real plan you'd be happy to sell, on a short, clear menu. A plan you'd never make, hidden details, or too many choices can trick or confuse buyers.

screens.setup: It's March. 20 families book party cakes each month. 16 choose cake only at ₹850, leaving you ₹450 each. 4 choose the full pack at ₹1,450, leaving you ₹750 each. That's ₹10,200 a month.
screens.question: How do you set your party menu?

options.label: Keep two plans and tell everyone about the full pack
options.outcome: You tell every family about the full pack. A few more agree: 6 of 20. You earn ₹10,800 a month, but every call takes more time.
options.why: Telling families about it helped a little. But they still compare ₹1,450 with ₹850, and the price difference looks big.
options.better: Add cake and cupcakes at ₹1,400, a real plan you'd be happy to sell.

options.label: Add eight more plans so everyone has a choice
options.outcome: Families look at the plans, ask questions, and say, "We'll think about it." Bookings fall from 20 to 15 a month, across many plans. You earn about ₹7,650 a month.
options.why: Too many choices made families wait instead of choosing. Like the jam test, fewer choices can lead to more sales.
options.better: Add cake and cupcakes at ₹1,400, a real plan you'd be happy to sell.

options.label: Add cake and cupcakes for ₹1,400
options.outcome: Now the full pack costs only ₹50 more than cake and cupcakes. 9 families choose it, 2 choose cake and cupcakes (you keep ₹740 from each), and 9 choose cake only. You earn ₹12,280 a month.
options.why: Your decoy is a real plan you're happy to sell. But its main job was to make the full pack look better. You earn the most from the full pack.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: Remember the line: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. A decoy is fair when it's a real option you'd be happy to sell, and you clearly say what each plan includes. This helps buyers see which plan gives them the most for their money.
A clearly ___ third choice helps sell the one ___ it.
screens.why: Correct. Print only helped sell print and web. Your ₹1,400 cake and cupcakes helps sell the ₹1,450 full pack.

summary: The decoy effect: a clearly worse choice makes the one next to it look like a good deal.
You'll see it in popcorn sizes and phone models. Ask: which choice is there just to make another look better?
Use it fairly: the decoy must be a real plan you'd be happy to sell, on a short, clear menu.

cards.front: Coffee: small ₹120, medium ₹200, large ₹220. Which is the decoy?
cards.back: Medium costs only ₹20 less than large. It makes large look like a good deal.

options: A real plan you'd be happy to sell
A plan you'd refuse to make
cards.back: A fair decoy is a real choice. A fake one looks like a trick when buyers notice it.

cards.front: You offer 10 tiffin plans, and many people leave without choosing. What should you do?
cards.back: Too many choices can stop people from buying. Keep the menu short and clear.

sources.label: Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational (2008), chapter 1: The Economist subscription test
Iyengar and Lepper, When choice is demotivating (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000)
